The decade commenced with the Franko-Prussian war, which ended in the humiliation of France and the extinction of the Napoleanic empire. he latter end of the decade witnessed a gigantic war between Russia and Turkey, resulting in the dismemberment of the latter and the political ascendancy of England in European politics through the sheer force of diplomacy. In Africa the aggressive policy of the British colony culminated in a war with the King of Zululand last year. The Zulus made a bold stand, and inflicted in the first instance a sigual defeat upon British arms, _Cetewayo, the hero of the Zula war, shewed a dash and vigour, which challenged admiration. In this war fell the last hope of the Napolean dynasty, The Prince Imperial, a fine young man, full of courage and enthusiasm, by way of some return for the hospitality of England, which had offered him and his Empress mother an asylum, volunteered his services in this war.

Thus was crushed in the bud the dearly cherished hope of the late Louis Napoleon, The news of the disaster, which befell British arms in Zululand, naturally enough filled England with grief and indignation, and called forth her highest energy. As might be expected she retrieved her honor in no time; Cetewayo was vanquished and deported to England. Durtne the last year there were numerous evidences that the bonds between England and India were drawing closer. Never before did the great Political Parties of the United Kingdom make India the subject of battle-cry in the same manner as they did during the past year. Both realized the great political significance of the Indian Dependency of England; both recognized that the sovereign country wielded serious responsibilities in that dependency, and both sought to give expression to their respective ideas of those responsibilities, but these ideas widely differed. The Conservatives have apparently forgotten their old traditions about Indian administration. Some of the most enlightened measures, which have emanated from the British Parliament regarding the administration of India - not the

have apparently forgotten their old traditions about Indian administration. Some of the most enlightened measures, which have emanated from the British Parliament regarding the administration of India - not the least of which was the gracious Proclamation of the Queen in 1858, justly considered the charter of the political and religious liberties of the princes and people of India, - were due to their counsel, to their advocacy, to their influence. But the times are out of joint. The Conservatives have now become the task-masters of India, They have been infected with the disease of Imperialism, and they do not scruple to stoop to any thing in order to carry ouf that grand idea. Before that altar they have sacrificed principle, honesty, humanity, and liberality, the generous instincts of the Englishman and the noble feclings of the British statesman. Some may attribute this difference to party feeling, others may lament that India should become the sport of party politics, but we for one rejoice that whatever the reasons the leaders of the Liberal party have taken India under their wings for shelter and protection, that they have lent their powerful intellects and still more powerful eloquence to the exposition of Indian wrongs and grievances at the bar of the English nation, that they sympathize with the myriad millions of this country and reprobate loudly, openly, and unflinchingly the policy of coercion and repression, which has of late unfortunately become the fashion.
